title: Amazon, Google Play destekli yeni Alexa Tablet serisini tanıttı
summary: Amazon, Fire OS yerine tam Android ve Google Play Store desteği sunan yeni Alexa Tablet ailesini duyurdu. Üç farklı modelden oluşan seri, yapay zeka asistanı Alexa+ ile öne çıkıyor.
body:
Amazon, Fire OS işletim sistemini geride bırakarak tamamen yenilenen ve Google Play Store erişimi sunan yeni Alexa Tablet serisini duyurdu. TechCrunch'ın aktardığına göre, aralarında amiral gemisi **Alexa Tablet 12 Pro**, Alexa Tablet 11 ve Alexa Tablet 8 modellerinin bulunduğu yeni seri, şirketin uygun fiyatlı cihaz stratejisinden farklı olarak daha iddialı bir donanım anlayışıyla geliştirildi.

## Üç yeni model ve teknik detaylar

Serinin en gelişmiş modeli olan Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, MediaTek Dimensity 8400 işlemci, 8GB veya 12GB RAM seçenekleri ve 12 inç büyüklüğünde 120Hz ekran yenileme hızı sunan 3:2 oranında bir ekrana sahip. Corning ile ortaklaşa geliştirilen ve yansımayı büyük ölçüde önleyen Nanomatte ekran seçeneği de 549,99 dolardan başlayan fiyatla sunuluyor. Ailenin diğer üyelerinden Alexa Tablet 11, 2,5K çözünürlüklü 11 inç ekranla 329,99 dolardan; daha kompakt tasarlanan Alexa Tablet 8 ise 8,7 inç ekranla 229,99 dolardan başlayan fiyatlarla listeleniyor. Cihazlar gücünü kişiselleştirilmiş zeka sunan **Alexa+** yapay zeka asistanından alıyor.

## Çıkış tarihi ve pazar planı

Serideki tüm tabletler ve çocuklara yönelik hazırlanan Amazon Kids sürümleri, 14 Ekim 2026'da ABD, Meksika ve Kanada'da satışa çıkacak. Cihazlar 19 Ekim'de ise İngiltere, Almanya, Fransa, İtalya ve İspanya'da raflardaki yerini alacak.

**Neden önemli?** Uzun yıllardır Fire OS tabanlı ve düşük bütçeli modellerle tablet pazarında yer alan Amazon, ilk kez tam Android deneyimi ve Google Play Store desteği sunan bu yeni seriyle doğrudan rekabetçi bir konuma gelmeyi hedefliyor.

source_texts.title: Amazon unveils new Alexa tablets with Alexa+ and Google Play Store access
source_texts.summary: The lineup includes three models: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and Amazon Alexa Tablet 8.
source_texts.text:
Amazon on Thursday unveiled a new lineup of Alexa tablets that feature personalized intelligence from its Alexa+ AI assistant and full access to the Google Play Store. The lineup includes three models: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and Amazon Alexa Tablet 8.
The tech giant says each tablet features an aluminum unibody design, high-resolution displays, and runs on Android. Plus, with access to the Google Play Store at launch, users will be able to download millions of apps, including YouTube, Netflix, Gmail, and more.
Until now, Amazon’s tablets have run Fire OS and ship with its own app store. With these new tablets, however, Amazon is taking a different approach to reach a wider audience. An Amazon spokesperson told TechCrunch that these are an all-new product line with new hardware and a new OS, rather than a rebrand of Fire Tablets.
The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro measures 6.5 mm thick and is engineered for “perfect balance,” Amazon explained in a press release. It houses a 12-inch, 280 PPI display, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 3:2 aspect ratio for more usable screen space, which the company says is perfect for reading, watching, or working. It comes in two display options: a standard display and a Nanomatte display with anti-glare.
Amazon says the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro delivers nearly three times the processing performance and nine times the graphics performance of any tablet it has shipped before. The company says the tablet can easily handle everything from multi-window multitasking and graphics-intensive gaming to 4K streaming. It features Dolby Atmos speakers, Wi-Fi 6E, and 16 hours of video playback.
The company also announced the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard, which Amazon says are designed to turn the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro into a full workstation.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99, while the Nanomatte model starts at $549.99. The tablet comes in Graphite.
The new tablets are launching with built-in access to Alexa+. Users will be able to say “Alexa” or tap the “Ask Alexa” button to get answers to questions, control their smart home, and more. With On-Screen Intelligence, users will be able to ask Alexa to look at what’s on screen to receive contextual help. For example, while browsing a list of trails, users can ask Alexa, “Which of these hikes is best for me?”
The Alexa Tablet 11 is an 11-inch device with a 2.5K display at 276 pixels per inch, 90Hz smooth scrolling, and a 16:10 aspect ratio. The tech giant says it’s designed for streaming, gaming, reading, and browsing. It features 15 hours of video playback and dual Dolby Atmos speakers. It starts at $329.99 and comes in Graphite, Amethyst, and Matcha.
The Alexa Tablet 8 is the smallest and most portable of the three, featuring an 8.7-inch display and an all-aluminum design that weighs 329 grams. It’s designed to be held in one hand and carried anywhere for reading, browsing, and streaming on the go, Amazon says. It starts at $229.99 and comes in Graphite, Rosette, and Teal.
All of the new tablets are launching with a new Kindle reading experience. When users open the Kindle app, notifications are silenced, blue light is reduced, and battery life can last up to 20 hours.
The company also announced on Wednesday that it’s launching new Amazon Kids tablets, with 8.7-inch and 11-inch sizes available. Bundles include a tablet, a kid-proof case, and a year of Amazon Kids+, which provides access to thousands of kid-friendly books, games, videos, and apps in an ad-free environment.
There are separate versions for pre-K kids (ages 3+) and kids 6+, as younger kids get a soft bumper case in designs from franchises like Paw Patrol and Barbie, while older kids get a slim hard case with a built-in kickstand.
All three Amazon Alexa Tablets and the Amazon Kids Tablets will go on sale October 14, 2026, in the U.S., Mexico, and Canada. They’ll launch in the UK, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain on October 19, while the Amazon Kids Tablets will also be available in Japan starting October 14.

source_texts.title: Hands-on with Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its wild new matte display
source_texts.summary: Amazon's Fire tablets are notable for being dirt cheap. While they're great for kids, they don't offer a premium Android tablet experience. The company's new $499 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is an attempt to build a device someone might actually want to use. It's one of a few new Android tablets Amazon announced today, and […]
source_texts.text:
Amazon’s Fire tablets are notable for being dirt cheap. While they’re great for kids, they don’t offer a premium Android tablet experience. The company’s new $499 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is an attempt to build a device someone might actually want to use. It’s one of a few new Android tablets Amazon announced today, and it’s the one you need to know about.
Hands-on with Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its wild new matte display
The Alexa line is also Amazon’s first tablet to run full-fledged Android with access to the Play Store.
Unlike the Fire Tablet lineup, the Alexa Tablet doesn’t run some hobbled version of Android stuck with Amazon’s app store with ads for Amazon services at every turn. It has full access to the Google Play app store. It’s powered by 8GB or 12GB of RAM with a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 8-core CPU. That’s more than enough for light gaming, powering Alexa, and running basic apps, but don’t expect Alien: Isolation to run super smoothly. The aluminum unibody feels great. It’s light at 550 grams (1.2 pounds), but not flimsy. It’s slightly lighter than the 13-inch iPad Air (617 grams) but heavier than the 11-inch (465 grams).
The screen is the truly exciting thing about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a 12.3-inch 3:2 display that can be configured with Corning’s Nanomatte tech, similar to Apple’s nano-texture, which reduces glare and gives the screen a more paper-like feel.
It’s impossible to do it justice in photos or video. The Nanomatte coating doesn’t simply reduce glare; it almost completely eliminates it. Amazon held a briefing in a brightly sunlit room, and I thought the 12 Pro was a dummy unit when I first saw it. It looked like a cardboard placeholder image was placed inside. Then an Amazon rep started swiping around the screen.
There’s also a standard glossy option, and the difference is shocking. In the bright sunlight of the room, the glossy screen was basically a mirror and was easily washed out when viewed at an angle. The Nanomatte display, however, was clearly readable at any angle and barely reflected any ambient light. Only at extreme angles in the brightest patches of light did it become difficult to see.
The screen pairs particularly well with the immersive Kindle mode. Here, background activities are limited, notifications are silenced, and blue light is lowered to reduce eye strain. There are three different Kindle-specific display modes. Standard delivers the full vibrancy of the screen; Color offers a softer, more muted experience; and Ink is full grayscale. In Kindle mode, battery life is also extended from 16 hours to 20 hours.
Without having the two side-by-side, it’s hard to say how it compares to Apple’s matte display on the iPad Pro, but anecdotally it seems to retain slightly more contrast. Using a stylus with it is much more pleasant than on a glossy display, but I can’t say I noticed a difference between it and an iPad.
The Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard attach magnetically and seem serviceable enough. I wouldn’t want to type on its shallow, cramped keys all day, but they’re fine for knocking out a few emails. The keyboard case was a little clunky to get on and off, though. It’s actually two parts — the back cover and stand are separate from the keyboard base.
Alexa Everywhere
The tablet shoves Alexa down your throat at every turn. In the bottom right-hand corner is an “Ask Alexa” bar that lets you quickly chat with the AI assistant. And in the top left-hand corner is what Amazon calls the Dynamic Tab. It offers up proactive suggestions from Alexa. That can be something as simple as picking up where you left off in a book or movie, or offering an itinerary for a three-day trip to New York. This is, of course, powered by Amazon’s deep well of information it gathers from your reading, viewing, and shopping habits.
Amazon keeps some of Alexa’s more invasive features off by default. On-Screen Intelligence, which can see what you’re doing and take actions based on what’s actually on your screen, is strictly opt-in. There are also robust controls for limiting what Alexa can hear and remember.
If you do opt in, though, Alexa becomes a pretty powerful shopping companion. I was able to open random photos from the internet and ask Alexa to find me something in them, like a coffee table or a mirror, and, even if it couldn’t track down the exact thing, it found something close. Then it would add it to my Amazon cart if I asked. How likely am I to ask Alexa to track down a bathroom fixture for me from a Pinterest photo and deliver it to my house in two days via Prime? Not very. I’m also unlikely to have it automatically add school holidays to my calendar from the Department of Education site, but it will if you ask it to.
The Alex Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99, but you’ll have to shell out at least $549.99 for the Nanomatte model. If you want to tack on the keyboard case and the Pro Pen, that will be an additional $149.99 and $89.99, respectively.
Amazon also announced two smaller models that lack the Nanomatte screen options. The Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $329.99, while the Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99. Those come in more fun colorways, including rosette and matcha, in addition to the drab but functional graphite of the Tablet 12 Pro.

source_texts.title: Amazon’s Alexa Tablets are coming for the iPad
source_texts.summary: Amazon is launching a new lineup of tablets that bear almost no resemblance to any tablet Amazon has ever launched before. They're not even called Fire, the name Amazon has used for its tablets for the last 15 years. They're called Alexa Tablets, and they're designed to do two things: bring Alexa Plus to the […]
source_texts.text:
Amazon is launching a new lineup of tablets that bear almost no resemblance to any tablet Amazon has ever launched before. They’re not even called Fire, the name Amazon has used for its tablets for the last 15 years. They’re called Alexa Tablets, and they’re designed to do two things: bring Alexa Plus to the center of your whole computing life, and be straight-up excellent tablets.
Amazon’s Alexa Tablets are coming for the iPad
They’re powerful, priced to move, and filled with AI ideas. Don’t you dare call them Fire tablets.
The most important thing about these new tablets’ software? They run Android. Full, Google Play-supported, all-the-apps Android. There are plenty of preloaded Amazon apps, of course, and some built-in ways to quickly access Prime Video content or shop for basically anything anywhere at any time, but it’s finally offering a proper Android experience. Panos Panay, Amazon’s SVP in charge of all things hardware and Alexa, tells me that “Google Play was a necessity, end of story.”
But Panay picked Android as the second most important thing about the Alexa Tablet. The first, he says, is the hardware. The Alexa Tablet is two and a half years in the making, Panay says, and he directed the team to start completely fresh in their tablet design. “Start from zero, don’t use any components we’ve ever used,” he says he told them. “Just ask, what is it? What is a great piece of hardware and what is it supposed to do?”
There are three devices in the Alexa Tablet lineup, all of which go on sale October 14th. The Tablet 8 has an 8.7-inch screen, starts at $229.99, and seems mostly designed for reading; the Tablet 11 has an 11-inch screen, starts at $329.99, and is more for watching stuff. They’re aimed squarely at the iPad Mini and base iPad, and seem nice enough. But the biggest device in the lineup, the one Panay really wants to tell me about, is the one he thinks really shows off what Amazon is doing here.
It’s called the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and it starts at $499. It’s 6.5mm thick and weighs 550 grams — a little thicker and a little lighter than the latest 13-inch iPad Pro — and comes with either 8 or 16 gigs of RAM and either 128 or 256 gigs of storage. It runs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, a chip you might have found in a high-end phone a year or so ago. All these specs are… fine. Good enough to run an Android tablet, but nothing to write home about.
The feature that really matters, Panay says, is the screen. Panay has this concept of the “one thing,” a single feature on a product that absolutely cannot be compromised on, no matter what. Make tradeoffs where you need to, he tells his team, but not on the one thing. “And the one thing on this product was, let’s go make the perfect screen.”
That screen is a 12.5-inch, 2800 x 1840 display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz and 500 nits of brightness. Its 3:2 aspect ratio, Panay says, is perfect for running two Android apps side by side. And on the most expensive, $549 model Alexa Tablet, the screen comes with what Amazon calls a Nanomatte display. The company partnered with Corning to actually etch a unique texture into the glass itself that is meant to be richer, higher contrast, and less prone to glare than a typical display. The process sounds similar to Apple’s excellent nano-texture finishes, but Amazon seems to believe its method comes with even fewer tradeoffs in contrast and sharpness. I haven’t seen the device in person yet, but The Verge’s Terrence O’Brien has, and it sounds like it has a chance to be as good as advertised.
The screen also adapts to what you’re doing on the tablet. If you launch the Kindle app, it turns off blue lights to make the reading experience warmer and more serene; if you start reading comics, it’ll render them extra glossy. Amazon understands well that tablets are primarily consumption devices — and the company is very happy to optimize for your time in Kindle and Prime Video.
The Alexa Tablet isn’t just for watching and reading, though. Amazon also made a keyboard case and a stylus, and Panay says he hopes people will use it as a secondary or even primary computer. He also hopes you’ll use it to do Alexa things. Amazon has been working on the LLM-powered version of its assistant for the last few years, and believes Alexa Plus can be more than just a smart home assistant. (Our testing suggests… otherwise.) You’ll be able to ask Alexa about anything you see on the screen, and the chatbot will try to offer recommendations, find information, and, of course, try to sell you anything it can find on Amazon.com. On these devices, Alexa Plus appears to be nearly as pervasive as Gemini or Siri on other tablets, and that’s precisely the point.
It has always made sense for Amazon to make tablets. But for so many years, the company that has seemed to be happy to simply make everything as cheap as possible in the hopes you’ll sign up for Prime and buy some stuff in the store. Trying to actually make great tablets seems new, and frankly a little surprising. But if it got the screen right, and made the right tradeoffs elsewhere, Amazon might finally have a proper iPad competitor.
